overview:
Right Knowledge (samyag‑jñāna) is one of the three jewels (ratnatraya) of Jainism, alongside Right Faith (samyag‑darśana) and Right Conduct (samyak‑cāritra). Together, these form the essential path to liberation (mokṣa) described across both Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions. In Jain epistemology, Right Knowledge is not merely the accumulation of information but the accurate, non‑distorted apprehension of reality as it truly is, free from doubt, misapprehension, and delusion.

Jain thinkers define Right Knowledge as knowledge that is true, certain, and aligned with the nature of substances (dravya), their qualities (guṇa), and their modes (paryāya). It is grounded in the recognition of the six fundamental substances—jīva, pudgala, dharma‑dravya, adharma‑dravya, ākāśa, and kāla—and the workings of karma that obscure the soul’s innate omniscience. Right Knowledge arises when karmic veils (jñānāvaraṇīya karma) are weakened, allowing the soul to perceive reality with increasing clarity.

Classical Jain texts describe five types of knowledge: mati‑jñāna (sensory‑mental knowledge), śruta‑jñāna (scriptural knowledge), avadhi‑jñāna (clairvoyance), manaḥparyāya‑jñāna (telepathy), and kevala‑jñāna (omniscience). Right Knowledge is not limited to any one of these; rather, it refers to the correctness and purity of whatever knowledge is present. Even scriptural knowledge becomes Right Knowledge only when accompanied by Right Faith and free from doubt or misinterpretation.

In practice, Right Knowledge includes understanding the vows (vratas), the nature of karma, the structure of the cosmos, and the ethical principles of nonviolence, non‑possessiveness, and restraint. Laypeople cultivate it through study (svādhyāya), reflection (anuprekṣā), and guidance from qualified teachers. Monastic traditions emphasize deeper scriptural mastery and meditative insight. Across Jain lineages, Right Knowledge is considered indispensable for spiritual progress, forming the bridge between correct perception and ethical transformation.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti/Umāsvāmi (accepted by both Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions)
primary_sources.translation: Right Faith, Right Knowledge, and Right Conduct are the path to liberation.
primary_sources.notes: This foundational aphorism (TS 1.1) establishes Right Knowledge as one of the three indispensable components of the liberation path. The text later elaborates on the five kinds of knowledge (TS 1.9–1.12).

primary_sources.title: Samayasāra
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Kundakunda (Digambara)
primary_sources.translation: Knowledge is that which knows; knowledge is that which illuminates.
primary_sources.notes: Kundakunda emphasizes the intrinsic luminosity of the soul’s knowledge and distinguishes pure knowledge from knowledge obscured by karmic bondage.

primary_sources.title: Pravacanasāra
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Kundakunda
primary_sources.translation: Faith is the quality of knowledge.
primary_sources.notes: This passage highlights the interdependence of Right Faith and Right Knowledge, showing that knowledge becomes ‘right’ only when accompanied by correct conviction.

primary_sources.title: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Śvetāmbara canonical text
primary_sources.original_text: जाणं च दंसणं च, उवओगं च तिहं गुणं
primary_sources.transliteration: jāṇaṃ ca daṃsaṇaṃ ca, uvayogaṃ ca tihaṃ guṇaṃ
primary_sources.translation: Knowledge, faith, and conduct—these three are the virtues.
primary_sources.notes: This text frequently pairs knowledge with faith and conduct, emphasizing its ethical and spiritual significance for both monastics and laypeople.

misconceptions.myth: Right Knowledge means possessing vast scriptural learning or intellectual mastery.
misconceptions.reality: Jain texts emphasize that Right Knowledge is correct, non‑deluded knowledge, not necessarily extensive knowledge. Even limited knowledge becomes ‘right’ when free from doubt, misinterpretation, and wrong belief.

misconceptions.myth: Right Knowledge is identical to omniscience (kevala‑jñāna).
misconceptions.reality: Right Knowledge refers to the correctness of any level of knowledge. Omniscience is the highest form of knowledge, but Right Knowledge can exist at lower levels such as sensory or scriptural knowledge.

misconceptions.myth: Right Knowledge can arise independently of ethical practice.
misconceptions.reality: Jain doctrine states that Right Knowledge is inseparable from Right Faith and Right Conduct. Ethical purification reduces karmic obstructions, enabling clearer and more accurate knowledge.
